crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing and adapting text, aims, budgets, and supporting materials from earlier grant applications to answer a new funding call.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must look, what it must contain, and how it must be submitted.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs in AI research grants cover the direct and indirect expenses that a sponsor will reimburse, from personnel salaries and fringe benefits to equipment, travel, materials, publication fees, and the compute and data storage that AI projects often require.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators for grant proposals is the work of identifying people, groups, and institutions whose expertise, resources, or access complements a proposed project.

children.name: Predicting Proposal Success
children.blurb: Predicting proposal success is the use of data and models to estimate whether a grant application will be funded, often before or during review.

sections.body: Grant writing is one of the places where language models have moved from demonstration to daily use. Researchers now ask AI systems to summarise their own prior papers into a background section, to reshape a draft into a funder's required structure, and to check a narrative against a call for proposals. The work is mostly text transformation and retrieval over a person's own publication record, not autonomous science. A model can pull a methods paragraph from an earlier paper and rewrite it for a new aim, or flag that a required section is missing. What it cannot do is decide whether the idea is worth funding, and it has no access to a review panel's judgement.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Drafting and formatting are the most reliable uses, because the source material is the researcher's own writing and the target format is published in the funder's rules. Budget work is narrower: models can check arithmetic, group costs into the categories a funder allows, and flag items that look unusual, but allowable cost rules vary by agency and change, so the final reading stays with a human. Finding collaborators is a search and matching problem, and it works best when the system has structured data about people, institutions and past projects rather than only prose. Predicting success is the weakest area. Review outcomes depend on panel composition, fit with a programme's priorities and factors that are not in any public record, so any score is a rough signal at best. Nothing here replaces the judgement of a research office or a principal investigator.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages follow the order a proposal actually takes shape. Drafting Proposals from Past Work is the starting point, for turning existing papers and results into a first narrative. Funder Formatting and Compliance comes next, for matching that narrative to a specific agency's structure and rules. Budgets and Allowable Costs sits alongside it, covering the numbers and the categories a funder will accept. Finding Collaborators moves outward from the text to the people, for assembling a team or locating complementary expertise. Predicting Proposal Success is the last page and the most speculative, for thinking about what signals correlate with funded proposals and where those signals stop being useful. Read together they cover the full path from an idea in a drawer to a submitted application.
